title: Straw dogs
hook: heaven and earth aren't sentimental; they treat things like straw dogs used in a ritual (Tao Te Ching 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter four: the Tao, empty like a bowl, and your line was untie the knot. Did one loop come loose? Today chapter five turns hard-edged, with one strange image. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

Does the rain know it's your wedding day? Months of planning. The chairs are out on the lawn, the flowers are tied to the ends of the rows, and at ten in the morning the sky opens. It's very hard not to take it personally. Why today? Why us? But the same rain is falling on the farmer who prayed for it, on the parking lot, on the stray cat under the porch. It isn't aimed. Chapter five of the Tao Te Ching says something blunt about this, and it uses a strange object to say it: a dog made of straw.
screen: `RAIN ON THE WEDDING.` → `WHY TODAY? WHY US?` → `IT ISN'T AIMED.`

segments.voice: First, heaven and earth aren't sentimental. The chapter opens by saying heaven and earth don't act out of a wish to be kind. In Legge's words, "they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with." And the sage, it says, treats people the same way. That can sound cold. Hold on to it a moment. Second, what a straw dog was. Another old Chinese book, the Zhuangzi, describes them. Before the ritual, the straw dogs were kept in fine boxes, wrapped in embroidered cloth, and handled with care by people who had fasted. After the offering, they were thrown out. People walked over them in the road, and grass-gatherers swept them up to burn. Honored, then discarded. Not out of spite. The ritual was simply over. Third, a bellows. Chapter five goes on to compare the space between heaven and earth to a bellows: empty, yet never used up, and the more it moves, the more comes out. The world isn't keeping score of anyone. It just keeps breathing. And the chapter adds a quiet warning: lots of talk wears out fast; better to keep to the center. Fourth, a neighbor with another spirit. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says God "sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." There, rain falling on everyone is a sign of the Father's goodness, and a reason to love even enemies. In chapter five, the same impartial rain is a sign that heaven isn't sentimental. Two traditions, two meanings, both looking at the same weather.
screen: `HEAVEN AND EARTH AREN'T SENTIMENTAL.` · `HONORED, THEN DISCARDED.` · `THE BELLOWS KEEPS BREATHING.` · `THE SAME RAIN, TWO MEANINGS.` · then, large: `NOT PERSONAL.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to accept one impersonal event. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that happened to you recently that wasn't aimed at you: the flight that was delayed, the cold that came the week of the trip, the price that went up. Notice the story your mind has wrapped around it, the why me. Now set the story down beside the event, and look at the event alone. The rain fell on everyone. If you pray, you can hold it in prayer just as it is. If you don't, breathe out, and let it be weather. The bell holds the time.
Straw dogs. Ritual figures, honored and then thrown away when the rite was over; chapter five says heaven and earth deal with all things like that. Today's word.
Your line: not personal. The next time today goes sideways, a spill, a red light, a cancellation, say it quietly before you react: not personal. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of chapter five sometimes use the straw dogs as a reminder that misfortune isn't aimed at them, letting events be what they are before deciding how to respond.

original.note: Chinese, chú gǒu: straw dogs, figures of straw used in a ritual and thrown away after.

trapdoor: what you thought: straw dogs means the universe is cruel.
what it means: heaven and earth aren't sentimental; they treat all things alike, as a ritual treats its straw figures, honored and then let go.
what a scholar hears: the Zhuangzi describes the custom: kept in boxes and embroidered cloth before the offering, trampled and burned after.
